questions.stem: The Maurya empire was founded in around 321 BCE by:
questions.explanation: Chandragupta Maurya — mentored by Chanakya (Kautilya) — overthrew the last Nanda king, Dhana Nanda, around 321 BCE and founded the Mauryan dynasty at Pataliputra. Bindusara was his son; Ashoka his grandson. Bimbisara had ruled Magadha three centuries earlier under the Haryanka dynasty. Greek sources knew Chandragupta as 'Sandrakottos'.

questions.stem: Ashoka's conversion to Buddhism was triggered by which war described in his 13th Rock Edict?
questions.explanation: The Kalinga War (c. 261 BCE) — Ashoka's bloody conquest of Kalinga (modern Odisha) — moved him to abandon violent conquest and adopt Buddhism, dhamma-vijaya (victory through righteousness), and a pan-imperial message of non-violence. Described in the 13th Rock Edict. The Battle of Hydaspes (326 BCE) was Alexander vs Porus. Taxila was Chandragupta's earlier campaign location, not a battle with Ashoka.

questions.stem: The 'Arthashastra', an ancient treatise on statecraft and economics, is attributed to:
questions.explanation: The Arthashastra — composed around the 4th century BCE — is attributed to Kautilya / Chanakya / Vishnugupta, who was Chandragupta Maurya's mentor and prime minister. It covers governance, military strategy, diplomacy, taxation, espionage and law. Panini wrote the Ashtadhyayi (Sanskrit grammar); Patanjali the Yoga Sutras; Kalidasa was a Gupta-age poet (Shakuntala, Meghaduta, Raghuvamsha).

questions.stem: The 'Golden Age of India' — a period of major cultural and scientific advance — is traditionally associated with the:
questions.explanation: Gupta era (~320-550 CE) — golden age in literature (Kalidasa), mathematics (Aryabhata — zero, decimal place-value, π ≈ 3.1416), astronomy (Varahamihira), medicine (Sushruta's Samhita was earlier but Gupta-age Charaka was codified), arts (Ajanta paintings) and Sanskrit drama. Mauryan empire produced the Arthashastra and Ashokan pillars; Cholas were much later (medieval Tamil dynasty); Kushans ruled ~1st-3rd century.

questions.stem: Samudragupta, often called the 'Napoleon of India' by the historian V. A. Smith, is chiefly praised for his:
questions.explanation: Samudragupta (c. 335-375 CE) — son of Chandragupta I — led extensive military campaigns across northern, eastern and southern India, recorded on the Allahabad Pillar Prashasti (composed by his court poet Harishena). He was also a noted vina player and is shown on some coins with that instrument. Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya), his son, is the one associated with a court of learning (Nine Jewels / Navaratnas).

questions.stem: The Chinese traveller Fa-Hien visited India during the reign of which Gupta ruler?
questions.explanation: Fa-Hien (Faxian) — Chinese Buddhist pilgrim — travelled in India from 399 to 414 CE during Chandragupta II's reign, seeking Buddhist scriptures. He described the prosperity and tolerant administration of the Guptas in his 'A Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms'. Hiuen Tsang (Xuanzang) came later, during Harshavardhana (7th century). I-Tsing came in the late 7th century.

questions.stem: The mathematician-astronomer Aryabhata, who lived during the Gupta age, is credited with:

options.option_text: Early use of zero and an approximation of π

questions.explanation: Aryabhata (b. 476 CE) wrote the Aryabhatiya (499 CE), which used place-value notation including a placeholder for zero (later formalised as a distinct number by Brahmagupta in 628 CE). He approximated π as 3.1416 and proposed that the Earth rotates on its own axis, causing the apparent motion of the stars. Penicillin was discovered by Fleming in 1928; the telescope by Galileo in 1609; the Charaka Samhita is a text on Ayurveda by Charaka (redacted c. 1st-2nd century CE).
